title: Bullying In The Classroom: The Ultimate Guide To Stopping It
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Framed as a comprehensive guide, this long-form piece lays out a full protocol for a classroom teacher to identify, stop, and follow up on bullying without waiting on administrators or counselors. It opens with a call to commit to protecting students and to understand what bullying actually is—the strong preying on the weak, physically or socially. The middle section walks through building a personal bullying policy that supplements the school's official policy, communicating it to students and parents in the first week of school, and supervising closely by watching body language and identifying vulnerable or isolated students. A large block of steps covers the response to an actual incident: gathering facts without overreacting, separating the bully immediately into time-out, notifying both sets of parents, using an extended one-week time-out with a written and recited apology, and checking in with both students and their families for weeks afterward. The piece closes by tying bullying prevention back to broader classroom-management fundamentals—clear accountability and a classroom students genuinely want to belong to—and ends with an appeal to protect students the way a parent would.
points: Have your own personal bullying policy on top of the school's official one, and send it home the first week of school.
Identify quiet, isolated, or socially vulnerable students early and build trusted 'eyes and ears' among class leaders.
When an incident occurs, gather facts calmly before reacting, then separate the bully into time-out immediately.
Use an extended one-week time-out with a written and recited apology as the consequence for bullying behavior.
Follow up with both the bullied student and the bully—and their parents—for weeks after the incident, not just once.
quotes: Bullying is the strong preying upon the weak. It can be a physical advantage or a social advantage. It can be one student or many.

Don’t wait for someone else to step in. Don’t assume that because you referred the bullying behavior to the principal or a counselor that it’s going to be taken care of. You take on the responsibility and see it through to the end.
Watch your class like a hawk. Always. Notice body language. Keep an eye on students who are socially awkward, smaller in stature, or less confident.
When you get a report of bullying, take your time gathering the facts. Take notes, interview witnesses, and open a file for documentation. Don’t be in a rush to react—and don’t overreact.
Keep the bullying student(s) in extended time-out for one week. Also, keep him (or her) with you, or under adult supervision, during recess.

The truth is, bullying rarely if ever happens in well-run classrooms. When standards of behavior are clearly communicated, when students are held accountable using an effective classroom management plan , and when the teacher is well-versed in fair, effective strategies, then students don’t bully.
Parents instinctively will do anything to protect their children. They’ll go to the ends of the earth to care for them. They’ll stand in front of anyone or anything wishing to harm them.
